text: Anne Legendre Armstrong (December 27, 1927 – July 30, 2008) was a United States diplomat and politician who made history as the first woman to serve as Counselor to the President and as United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom. She held these positions under the administrations of Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, and Jimmy Carter. Armstrong was born on December 27, 1927, in New Orleans, Louisiana, and graduated from Vassar College in 1949. She married Tobin Armstrong, a cattle rancher from Texas, in 1950. From 1966 to 1968, she served as vice chairman of the Texas Republican Party, and from 1971 to 1973, she was co-chairman of the Republican National Committee. She delivered the keynote address at the 1972 Republican National Convention, becoming the first woman from either major party to do so. On December 16, 1972, at a White House Christmas dinner, she praised both "Jesus Christ, the Prince of Peace" and President Nixon, who had ordered the Christmas Bombing of North Vietnam, in the same breath. Nixon appointed her Counselor to the President on December 19, 1972, a role she held from January 19, 1973, to November 1974 under President Ford. During her time as Counselor, she founded the first Office of Women's Programs in the White House, which preceded the current White House Council on Women and Girls. Fluent in Spanish, she served as Nixon’s liaison to Hispanic Americans and was a member of a Cabinet committee on opportunities for Spanish-speaking people. From 1976 to 1977, she was the first woman to serve as United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom. At the 1976 Republican National Convention in Kansas City, Missouri, there was a draft effort to nominate her as vice presidential candidate with President Gerald Ford, but Senator Robert Dole was selected instead. In 1978, she supported George W. Bush in his successful primary challenge to Jim Reese in Texas's 19th congressional district. Armstrong was a strong advocate for the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), stating in 1971 that it had become a symbol of meaning for many and would resolve numerous legal questions. In 1987, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Ronald Reagan. In 1989, she was awarded the Golden Plate Award by the American Academy of Achievement. She also received an honorary Doctor of Laws from St. Mary's University in 1978. Armstrong died of cancer in 2008 and is buried at Oakwood Cemetery in Austin, Texas.
